subtype: Approach: envelope-style split into separate accounts [Action]
passage: Note from the first-job orientation mentor. Rafiq joined the company in July and I watched how the salary was handled on the first day it arrived. Within two hours Rafiq had moved money into three places: a bills account that pays rent and the phone, a spending wallet for food and outings, and a savings pot. Madhuri, another new joiner, asked what happens when the wallet runs out early. "Then I wait," Rafiq said. "I don't touch the other two." By the last week of the month the wallet was empty and Rafiq walked to the office instead of taking the auto. It was a small inconvenience. I noted that the bills were paid on time and the savings pot had not moved.

qa.q: How many places did Rafiq split the salary into?
qa.a: Rafiq split the salary into three places: a bills account, a spending wallet and a savings pot.

qa.q: What did Rafiq mean by saying I wait when the wallet was empty?
qa.a: Rafiq felt firm and unbothered, meaning that Rafiq would not dip into the other two pots and would put up with the inconvenience until next month.

qa.q: What could Rafiq do if the spending wallet is always empty early, and why?
qa.a: Rafiq could adjust the wallet's share slightly after two months of data, because the split should match real needs.

qa.q: How might Madhuri see Rafiq's rule of waiting?
qa.a: Madhuri seems curious, and may find it strict but clear, since the other pots stay safe.

grounding: A new employee divides the salary the same day into a bills account, a spending wallet and a savings pot, and waits when the wallet is empty.
